segments.text: This is Notch. It's a desktop app that answers one question about your infrastructure: what does this repository actually need, and what is actually deployed? Everything you're about to see is running against a real Zerops account over the real API. Nothing here is mocked.

It starts with a Zerops personal access token. Notch verifies it by making a real call, not by checking that it looks like a token. The token is held in the daemon's memory for this session only. It is never written to disk, never logged, and never sent anywhere but Zerops.
We're in. Notch has read the account and found the projects on it. The bar across the top is the whole application: pick a project, point at a repository, and scan.

Let's start from nothing and create a project. Notch is explicit that this makes a real, billable project on your account, and that it starts empty. Creating infrastructure and filling it are two separate decisions, so they are two separate buttons.

Now the repository we want to deploy. Point Notch at any folder on this machine. In the desktop build there's also a real folder picker, and that is the only native capability the shell exposes — no file system access, no shell, just a path you chose yourself.

This is a Node API that needs Postgres for records, Valkey for sessions, Meilisearch for search, Qdrant for embeddings, NATS for jobs, and object storage for uploads. Notch reads the package manifest and the environment files, and compares what it finds against what the project actually runs.

Seven services missing, and they're drawn on the architecture canvas as dashed ghosts rather than hidden in a list. The gap between your repository and your infrastructure is a shape, and a shape is easier to act on than a bullet point.

Every finding cites its evidence. Meilisearch is here because the code depends on the meilisearch client in package dot json. Notch never asserts a requirement it cannot point at a line for, and anything inferred only from an environment variable name is marked low confidence, because a name is weaker evidence than an import.

Now scan it a second time, and Notch says something a live view cannot: these have been missing across two scans, since the first time we looked. That a service is missing right now is something anyone can compute. That it has been missing since the last time you checked requires having written the earlier answer down. This is the reason Notch keeps a database at all.

Provisioning shows you the exact import file before anything is written. A button that creates real infrastructure should never be the first time you learn what it creates, so the preview and the write are built by the same code and cannot drift apart.

Notch also found nine secrets by name in the environment files, and declared them on the runtime service. Look closely at the values: they are Zerops generator expressions, not secrets. The real values are generated by the platform during the import, so nothing is copied out of your repository and no secret ever appears in this file.
Confirm, and Notch sends the import. These are real services being created on a real account.

Six of the seven are now satisfied. The seventh, object storage, has no matching Zerops service type — so it stays a ghost and says so, rather than being quietly dropped to make the number look better.

And here is the architecture, re-read from the platform rather than assumed. The runtime on top, the data stores beneath it, the message queue below that, with the real ports Zerops assigned. These cards are not a diagram of what we asked for. They are a picture of what exists.

The timeline is the half a live view cannot give you. It survives a reload and a daemon restart, because it is in Postgres. You can see the scan that found seven gaps, the single writer lock being taken so two people cannot provision the same project at once, and the import that succeeded.

Finally, Notch writes the work back to disk as a zerops dot yaml you can commit. Every service carries the reason it is there as a comment, so a reviewer sees the evidence in the pull request without needing Notch open at all.

That's Notch. Paste a token, point at a repository, and see the difference between what your code needs and what your infrastructure has — with the evidence for every claim, a history that remembers, and a file you can commit. Thanks for watching.
